opus-5.5.text:
Part of it is just that a lot of the public conversation about language models has been bottlenecked on words that nobody has pinned down. People ask whether a model "understands" language, or "has a world model," or "reasons," and then two people argue past each other for an hour because one has a behavioral notion in mind and the other has something closer to an internal-representation notion. Neither is wrong exactly, but you can't make progress if you haven't said which question you're asking.

So when I approach these questions, I try to turn the vague word into something you could actually test. If I want to know whether a model represents the state of the world described in a piece of text, I need to say what "the state" is, what it would mean for that information to be encoded somewhere, and what experiment would distinguish a model that has it from one that's exploiting surface statistics. Once you've written that down, you can be wrong in an informative way. Before that, you can't even be wrong.

The other reason is that these systems are very good at producing behavior that looks impressive under a loose definition. If your evaluation is "does the output seem sensible to me," you'll find intelligence everywhere, and you'll also miss failures that only show up when you push on a specific capability. A well-formulated task forces you to decide in advance what counts as success, and that protects you from both over-claiming and under-claiming.

And I'd say there's a kind of intellectual honesty piece too. A defensible definition is one you'd be willing to defend against someone who disagrees with your conclusion. If the definition only works because it was tuned to give the answer you wanted, that's not really science. Starting from clear tasks is how you make the results mean something to people outside your own head, including people who are skeptical, and those are exactly the people you most need to convince.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers must define terms and formulate testable tasks, but it does not state that inspecting language models alone is insufficient to determine those definitions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that a lot of the questions people want to ask about language models right now are questions where the words doing the heavy lifting don't actually have agreed-upon meanings. Does the model "understand" anything? Does it "know" facts? Does it have "beliefs" or "goals" or "intentions"? Those are the questions that motivate a lot of the field, and they're the questions that make the public care, but you can't run an experiment on "understanding" directly. You have to first say what it would mean, operationally, for a system to understand something, and then you have to be willing to defend that definition against people who think you've picked something too easy or too hard.

The reason I think that step matters so much is that we've seen what happens when it gets skipped. You get a paper that shows a model failing some cleverly constructed test and concludes it has no world model, and then a week later someone shows the same model succeeding on a slightly different version and concludes the opposite. Both groups are often reporting real empirical findings. What they're disagreeing about is not the data, it's what the data is supposed to be evidence for. And if that disagreement is never made explicit, the field just goes around in circles, with everyone quietly using their own private definition and talking past each other.

So when I say well-formulated tasks, I mean something fairly concrete. If I claim a model represents the state of the world described in a text, I should be able to say what representation I'm looking for, what it would mean to find it, and what result would have convinced me I was wrong. Then I can do the work of building a probe or an intervention and actually testing it. The nice thing about that discipline is that it tends to generate smaller, more specific, more falsifiable claims. Instead of "does the model understand language," you end up asking "does the model track the location of this object across these sentences, and does that internal representation causally influence what it says next." That question is less exciting, but you can actually answer it, and the answers accumulate.

There's also an intellectual-honesty dimension. A lot of the vocabulary we use for these systems is borrowed from how we talk about people, and that borrowing is doing a lot of hidden argumentative work. When I say a model "believes" something, I'm importing a whole theory of mind that may or may not fit. Having to define the term forces you to notice what you're importing and decide whether you actually want it. Sometimes you find the human concept carves up the space in a useful way for machines, and sometimes you find it doesn't, and either outcome is informative.

I'd also say this is just how the rest of cognitive science learned to operate. Psychologists stopped arguing about whether animals "really" have concepts in the abstract and started designing tasks where you could say exactly what behavior counts as evidence. That shift is what made the field cumulative. I think language model research is at the point where it needs to make the same move. The models are interesting enough and consequential enough that we can't afford to keep having arguments where nobody can lose.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers must define terms such as “understanding” operationally before testing models, but it does not state that inspecting language models alone is insufficient to determine those definitions.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very easy to ask a question like, “Does a language model understand language?” and have two people give opposite answers while agreeing about everything the model actually does. They’re just using different definitions of understanding. If we want to make scientific progress, we need to turn those questions into claims that evidence could support or rule out.

A well-formulated task gives you a way to do that. What information does the model get? What are we asking it to predict or accomplish? What would count as success? And then, crucially, what does success on that task actually tell us? If a model answers a question correctly, that’s an observation. Whether it demonstrates some broader capacity depends on how the task was constructed and what alternative explanations you’ve excluded.

That doesn’t mean we should only study things that are easy to measure. It means we need to be explicit about the relationship between what we can measure and the bigger question we care about. Otherwise, we can build increasingly impressive systems without getting much clearer about what we’ve learned from them.

r001.rationale: The response explains that people can agree on everything a model does yet disagree about whether it understands language because they use different definitions. This communicates that inspecting the model’s behavior alone cannot settle the definitions used to study it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic issue is that a lot of the words we use to describe language models—understanding, reasoning, knowledge—are words that carry a huge amount of baggage. If I say a model understands something, you might have a very different idea of what that means than I do. And then we can look at exactly the same experimental result and draw completely different conclusions.

So I find it useful to start by asking: what is the actual capability we’re interested in? What information does the model get, what does it have to produce, and what would count as evidence that it’s doing the thing we care about? That forces us to turn a broad intuition into a question we can actually investigate.

Of course, a well-defined task isn’t automatically a good proxy for understanding or intelligence. You still have to defend that connection. But at least it gives us something concrete to disagree about, and a way to make progress beyond arguing about what a word means.

r001.rationale: The response says broad terms need operational definitions and that tasks provide concrete questions, but it does not state that inspecting language models alone is insufficient to determine those definitions.
